notes.meaning: The Pharisees heard that more people were following Jesus than John the Baptist. Jesus knew about this without anyone telling Him, which is why John calls Him "the Lord" here. The Pharisees were jealous and suspicious. The good news spreading often makes its enemies angry.

John adds a small correction: Jesus did not baptize people Himself. His disciples did. Older writers give several reasons. Preaching was the greater work. It honored and trained the disciples. It also kept people from boasting that Jesus had baptized them, and from splitting into groups over it.

differ.view: A baptism done by Christ's servants is truly Christ's own baptism. Its power to wash and renew comes from Him, not from the person who performs it.
The verse shows that baptism itself does not save. It is an act of obedience and a public witness to faith.

notes.meaning: Jesus left Judea and went back north to Galilee. The Pharisees' anger was growing, and the time for His death had not yet come. So He moved away from needless danger. We should not be scared away from our duty, but we should not rush into danger either.

Samaria lay right between Judea and Galilee, so the direct road went through it. Many Jews took a longer road around it to avoid Samaritans. Some writers also see a deeper reason: Jesus "had to" go because a needy soul was waiting there.
Sychar was probably the old town of Shechem, a place with a long Bible history. Nearby was land Jacob had given to his son Joseph (Genesis 48:22). Joseph's bones were later buried there.

Jesus was truly tired from walking, so He sat down by Jacob's well. This shows He was a real human being who felt our weakness, so He can feel for us (Hebrews 4:15). He walked everywhere and had no comfortable seat. The "sixth hour" was about noon, the hot middle of the day.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think John counts hours the Roman way, so the "sixth hour" would be about 6 in the evening. That was a usual time for drawing water.

notes.meaning: A Samaritan woman came to get water, and Jesus asked her for a drink. He really was thirsty. But He also used the moment to begin a talk about God, putting her good ahead of His own needs. He was willing to accept help from someone others looked down on.
John explains that the disciples had gone into town to buy food. That is why Jesus was alone and asked the woman for help. It also left room for a quiet, private talk with her.

The woman was surprised. Jews and Samaritans hated each other, partly over where God should be worshiped. Jews would not accept favors from Samaritans or share their cups. Jesus did not show the bitterness of His own people. That made her wonder about Him.

Jesus turned the talk from ordinary water to God's gift. The gift is Jesus Himself, the free gift of God's love. "Living water" normally meant fresh running spring water. Jesus uses it to mean the Holy Spirit, who gives new life (see John 7:38-39). If she knew who He was, she would ask, and He would give.

She pointed out that He had no bucket or rope, and the well was very deep. She took His words about water in a plain, earthly way. Some think she was teasing Him for promising more than He could give.

She asked if He thought He was greater than Jacob, who gave them the well. Samaritans claimed Jacob as their forefather. Without knowing it, she was comparing the servant to the Master. Jesus truly is greater than Jacob.

Jesus did not argue about Jacob. He simply said that anyone who drinks this water will get thirsty again. In the same way, the comforts of this world satisfy only for a little while. Then we need more.

The water Jesus gives never runs out. It becomes a spring inside the person, bubbling up and leading to eternal life. This is the Holy Spirit living in the believer. Believers may still long for more of God, but they will never be left dry. If you feel thirsty again, keep coming to Christ.

The woman asked for this water, but mainly so she would not have to keep walking to the well. She was still thinking about earthly needs, not eternal life. Even so, she felt a curious longing for whatever this stranger was offering.

Jesus suddenly told her to call her husband. This was not changing the subject. He was gently waking up her conscience, so she would see her sin. A person needs to see they are lost before they see why they need a Savior.
She answered, "I have no husband," probably hoping to end that topic. Jesus kindly agreed that her words were true. Even when He spoke hard truth, He was courteous.

Jesus showed He knew her whole story: she had had five husbands, and the man she lived with now was not her husband. He spoke mildly and did not call her names. He let her own conscience do the rest. Kind correction often helps more than harsh words.
Amazed that He knew her life, she said He must be a prophet, someone sent by God. She did not deny what He said. She began to treat Him with respect.

She raised the big argument between Samaritans and Jews. Samaritans worshiped on nearby Mount Gerizim, where they had built a temple. Jews said Jerusalem was God's chosen place. Many writers think she was trying to move away from her own sin. Others think she sincerely wanted to know how to worship God rightly.

Jesus said a time was coming when the place of worship would no longer matter. People would worship God as Father anywhere, not just on one mountain or in one city. The old system of the Jewish temple was about to pass away.

Jesus said the Samaritans worshiped without truly knowing God. They accepted only the five books of Moses and had mixed in other ideas. The Jews had God's fuller word. Salvation comes from the Jews, because the Savior was born a Jew and the message spread from them to the world.

That new time had already begun with Jesus. True worship is "in spirit": from the heart, helped by the Holy Spirit, not just outward ceremony. It is "in truth": sincere, and the real thing that the old sacrifices only pointed to. The Father is looking for people who worship Him this way.
God is Spirit. He has no body and is not limited to one place. So our worship must fit who He is. It must come from the heart and be real, not just outward show.

The woman said she knew the Messiah was coming. He would explain everything. ("Messiah" and "Christ" both mean God's promised, anointed Savior. John added the word "Christ" for his readers.) Samaritans expected Him from promises in the books of Moses, such as Deuteronomy 18:15.

Jesus told her plainly, "I am He." This was one of the first times He openly said He was the Messiah. He told a despised Samaritan woman more clearly than He had yet told His own disciples. No past sin can keep someone from Him who humbly trusts Him.

The disciples came back and were surprised to find Him talking with a woman. Jewish teachers usually avoided this, especially with a Samaritan. Yet no one questioned Him, because they trusted He had a good reason. When we don't understand what Jesus does, we can still trust Him.
